Day 1 – Data & Domain¶

Use Case¶

In the context of alpine wildlife monitoring and automated population census programs, images are generated by camera traps and telephoto lenses and captured using trail cameras and digital DSLR sensors deployed across the Swiss National Park and protected alpine zones (e.g., Graubünden, Valais) in order to non-invasively detect, classify, and count Alpine ibex (Capra ibex, Steinbock) individuals. These images are used by wildlife biologists, conservation authorities (e.g., KORA, Swiss National Park rangers), and cantonal hunting offices to perform population estimates, behavioural analysis, and habitat-use assessments. This use case is particularly relevant for Switzerland because the Alpine ibex was once extinct in the wild and was reintroduced exclusively through the Swiss National Park from 1920 onward; its monitoring is mandated under Swiss federal nature protection law (NHG / JSG) across steep, remote alpine terrain where manual survey is unfeasible, making automated image-based detection the primary scalable monitoring tool.

Problem Statement¶

This project addresses the problem of limited intra-class visual variability caused by sparse camera trap acquisition, compounded by extreme alpine lighting conditions — including harsh midday shadows cast by rock faces, high-contrast snow-to-shadow transitions, and flat diffuse overcast illumination — within the context of automated Alpine ibex detection. If a detection model is trained exclusively on images from a single season or time of day, domain shift between summer granite-dominated backgrounds and winter snow-covered terrain may arise, leading to degraded detection performance and increased false-negative rates on out-of-distribution field images. Preserving the fine-grained texture contrast at the boundary between the ibex’s dark, coarse fur coat and the high-reflectance rocky background is essential for reliable species discrimination in this use case, as this boundary constitutes the primary high-frequency edge signal used by image classifiers to localise and identify the animal.

Experimental Objective¶

The objective of this project is to investigate how varying alpine environmental conditions — specifically differences in background texture, illumination angle, and seasonal appearance — influence the visual distinctiveness of the fur–rock boundary region within the context of automated ibex monitoring, in order to better understand which image properties must be preserved or synthetically diversified through augmentation to maintain classifier robustness across the full range of real-world deployment conditions encountered in Swiss alpine terrain.

Data Definition, Source, and Visualization¶

The selected image represents an Alpine ibex (Capra ibex, Steinbock) photographed in its natural mountain habitat in the Swiss Alps, captured using a consumer digital camera and stored in JFIF format, expressed in the RGB colour space after conversion. Its relevant visual characteristics include a rich, coarse fur texture with visible directional strand patterns on the animal’s body, sharp luminance edges along the fur–rock and fur–sky boundary, moderate-to-high chromatic contrast between the dark brown-grey pelage and the lighter granite rock surface, strong directional shading gradients from direct alpine sunlight producing both specular highlights on exposed rock and deep shadow regions within fur folds, and spatial resolution sufficient to resolve individual fur texture elements — all of which are important for an augmentation strategy that must broaden the training distribution while preserving the species-identifying edge and texture structures. The data originate from a personal photograph taken in the Swiss Alps and are appropriate because they reflect the exact sensor and lighting conditions (consumer camera, unconstrained outdoor illumination, high-altitude alpine setting) representative of field monitoring scenarios, and they contain the high-frequency boundary and texture signals identified in the problem statement as central to this use case.

In [5]:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image

# Load image
img_path = "Data/Steinbock.jpg"
img_pil = Image.open(img_path).convert("RGB")
img = np.array(img_pil)

# rotate image by 90 degrees clockwise
img = np.rot90(img, k=-1)

# Inspect
print(f"Shape : {img.shape}  (height x width x channels)")
print(f"Dtype : {img.dtype}")
print(f"Min   : {img.min()}")
print(f"Max   : {img.max()}")

# Display full image
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.imshow(img)
ax.set_title("Mountain Goat — Swiss Alps (Original)", fontsize=13)
ax.set_xlabel("x (pixels)")
ax.set_ylabel("y (pixels)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Shape : (4032, 3024, 3)  (height x width x channels)
Dtype : uint8
Min   : 0
Max   : 255

Observations: The visualization illustrates a full-body view of an Alpine ibex standing on rocky alpine terrain, with notable high-contrast luminance edges observed along the boundary between the animal’s dark, coarse fur coat and the lighter-toned granite rock surface. Strong directional shading gradients from direct alpine sunlight are visible across both the fur and the surrounding rock, producing specular highlights on exposed stone faces and deep shadow regions within the fur folds — the exact challenging conditions identified in the problem statement. The spatial resolution is sufficient to resolve individual fur texture elements, confirming that this image contains the high-frequency edge and texture structures that are central to the defined use case of automated ibex detection under variable alpine lighting conditions.

In [6]:
# ROI crop: fur–rock boundary region on the ibex's body
# Targets the central body area where the dark fur coat transitions
# to the lighter rocky background — the key structure from the problem statement.

h, w, _ = img.shape
y0, y1 = int(h * 0.20), int(h * 0.70)
x0, x1 = int(w * 0.20), int(w * 0.80)
roi = img[y0:y1, x0:x1]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

axes[0].imshow(img)
axes[0].add_patch(
    plt.Rectangle((x0, y0), x1 - x0, y1 - y0,
                  edgecolor='red', facecolor='none', linewidth=2.5)
)
axes[0].set_title("Mountain Goat — Swiss Alps (Original, ROI marked)", fontsize=11)
axes[0].set_xlabel("x (pixels)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("y (pixels)")

axes[1].imshow(roi)
axes[1].set_title("ROI: Fur–Rock Boundary — Key Structure", fontsize=11)
axes[1].set_xlabel("x (pixels)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("y (pixels)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations (ROI): This region was selected because it contains the highest-density concentration of the fur–rock boundary contrast — the precise structure identified in the problem statement as essential for reliable ibex detection under variable alpine lighting. Within the crop, the coarse, directional texture of the ibex’s dark fur is clearly distinguishable from the granular, lighter-toned granite surface, and the sharp luminance edge at their boundary is unambiguously visible. This boundary is the image feature most susceptible to degradation under the challenging illumination conditions described in the problem statement (harsh shadows, glare on rock, seasonal background change), making it the primary structure around which the augmentation objective of this project is organised — understanding how synthetic image variation can broaden training distribution while keeping this discriminative edge-and-texture signal intact.
